  Thanks for the article.
  Yes, the Irish were treated very badly not just in the USA. It was the same in England and Canada. And I’m sure in other countries
  such as Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. It was kind of sad especially for many as their living conditions were awful in Ireland,
  both in rural areas and in towns and cities especially Dublin and when they arrived in their new homeland, it was probably much of the
  same - abject poverty. At one time, believe it was in the Victorian Era, Dublin’s slums were the worst in Europe. They were still pretty
  bad until the 1940s. Many blame the British and their Penal Laws for oppressing the Irish. If you haven’t read about the Penal Laws, it’s
  a must read in understanding the Irish and their history. It’s also why Irish genealogy is so hard; the Catholic Church wasn’t allowed to
  keep records as they weren’t the official church, The Church of Ireland was. The interesting phenomenon is that the Irish were
  basically a rural society and when they emigrated to other countries, they became the cheap labourers but within an urban setting. It
  must have been so disorienting and a huge paradigm shift for them. I do believe in PTSD and inter-generational trauma and the ‘An
  Gorta Mor’ had a huge negative impact on the psyche and morale of the Irish. A few personal examples : One time I went grocery
  shopping with my grandfather b. 1893 and I’ll never forget how he inspected every single potato before he put it in the bag. He also
  had an attitude found in the Irish of how you had to stay in your place, breaking out and being successful was frowned up and I saw its
  affect on my Dad, not so much his younger brother. And this was coming from my Granda who had a good education and training for
  someone of his generation. The fear of being alienated or shunned by your own people was real. And of course, let’s not get into what
  the Catholic Church has done to Ireland and its people. The control they had over the people was crippling, destructive and
  dysfunctional. The British and then Eamon de Valera as the first president of the Free Irish State and the Republic allowed that to
  happen. They passed off a lot of governmental and societal responsibilities to them. Anyway, when the Irish Catholics came to the
  USA and Canada part of the discrimination against them was religious, people of British and Scots-Irish background were already
  established and they were Protestant. There’s an article I read about Philadelphia. The Scots-Irish were well established in the city
  after arriving in the late 1700s/ early 1800s and were very prejudiced against the Irish Catholics. I shared it with a Tracey cousin whose
  2x Gt.grandfather, my gt. Grandmother’s brother, went to Philadelphia in the early 1880s and he acknowledged his ancestors had a
  hard time. Even in Canada, the Orangemen were very influential in Toronto and that’s why many Irish, like my grandparents and Dad
  went to Montreal. They could still get jobs in English in Montreal and being Catholic wasn’t perceived as a problem. Thank goodness,
  that has all changed.
